Daily deep-dive · Day 2

Bloom Filters

A tiny bit array that can tell you something is definitely not in a set, or probably is — using a fraction of the memory of storing the items themselves.

01The problem, in plain words

You want to answer one cheap question over and over: "Is this item possibly in my set, or definitely not?" — using a small, fixed amount of memory no matter how many items you've added.

Why does the "definitely not" answer matter so much? Because it lets you skip expensive work. A database checks a Bloom filter before reading from disk: if it says "this key is definitely not in this file," the slow disk read is skipped entirely. A memory check is roughly 100,000× faster than a disk read, so avoiding even a fraction of those reads is a massive win.

Analogy: a nightclub bouncer with a bad memory but a clever stamp system. Instead of remembering every face, he presses a few overlapping rubber stamps onto each guest's hand on the way in. Later he can check a hand for those stamp marks. No marks where he'd expect them? You were definitely never stamped — you're not on the list. All the marks present? You're probably a guest… though by sheer luck another guest's stamps might have left the same marks.

02The core mechanism

You keep one array of m bits, all starting at 0, plus k independent hash functions. Each hash function maps an item to a position in the array.

Add an item: run it through all k hash functions to get k positions, and set those bits to 1.
Test an item: hash it the same way and look at those k bits.
Any bit is 0 → the item is definitely not present. (If you'd added it, all k bits would be 1. A single zero is proof of absence.)
All bits are 1 → the item is probably present. You either added it, or other items happened to set those same bits. This is a false positive.
guaranteed No false negatives

It never says "not here" about something that is here. A "definitely not" is always trustworthy.

accepted cost Possible false positives

It occasionally says "probably here" about something that isn't. You tune how often this happens.

That asymmetry is the entire point. The error only ever happens in the safe direction: a "maybe" just makes you do the work you'd have done anyway — you're never wrong in a way that loses data.

03Key terminology

Bit array (size m)
The fixed block of m bits that is the filter. It never grows as you add items — only more bits flip from 0 to 1. Why it matters: memory is decided up front and stays flat. That predictability is why it scales to billions of items.
Hash functions (count k)
The k independent functions that each map an item to one position. In practice they're often derived cheaply from two base hashes rather than computing k separate ones. Why it matters: k is a dial. Too few and bits aren't distinctive; too many and the array fills up fast. There's a sweet spot.
False positive rate (FPR)
The probability the filter says "probably present" for an item you never added. Approximately (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k, where n is the number of items added. Why it matters: this is the knob you actually care about. More bits per item drives it down; it's how you trade memory for accuracy.
Bits per item (m / n)
How much room each item gets. A common tuning is ~10 bits per item with k ≈ 7, giving roughly a 1% false-positive rate. Why it matters: ~10 bits ≈ 1.25 bytes can stand in for a multi-kilobyte row. That compression is the whole appeal.
Optimal k
For a chosen size and item count, the false-positive rate is minimized at k = (m / n) × ln 2. Why it matters: you don't guess the number of hash functions — once you pick a size and expected load, the best k falls out of a formula.
Counting Bloom filter
A variant where each slot is a small counter instead of a single bit: add increments, delete decrements. Why it matters: it's the standard way to make deletion safe (see the limitation below), at the cost of extra memory per slot.

04The two big limitations

You can't delete (in the basic version). Clearing an item's bits might clear a bit another item relies on — which would create a false negative, the one error a Bloom filter promises never to make. The fix is the counting Bloom filter.
You can't read anything back. It only answers yes/no membership. You can't list its contents or retrieve a value. It's a gatekeeper, not a container.
Accuracy degrades as it fills. Add far more items than you sized it for and the false-positive rate climbs toward useless. Size it for your expected load, or use a scalable variant.

05Where it's used

SystemHow it uses the idea
Cassandra / RocksDB / LevelDBEach on-disk SSTable has a Bloom filter; a "definitely not" lets the engine skip reading that file when looking up a key.
CDNs & caches"One-hit-wonder" filtering — only cache an object on its second request, so single-access junk never pollutes the cache.
Browsers / securityEarly Google Safe Browsing checked URLs against a local malware-list filter before making any network call.
Distributed systemsSummarize "which keys do I hold?" to a peer compactly, without shipping the entire key set.

06Cousins worth knowing

StructureWhat's different
Cuckoo filterSupports deletion and often uses less space at low false-positive rates.
Scalable Bloom filterGrows automatically when you exceed the item count you planned for.
HyperLogLogAnswers a different question — how many distinct items, not membership — with similarly tiny memory.

07Common confusions

"Probably present" is not "present." An all-ones result is a hint, not a confirmation. If you need certainty, the filter only saves you the lookups it rules out.
It doesn't store the items. There's no way to recover what was added — only bits are kept, and many items can share the same bits.

08One-sentence summary

A Bloom filter is a small bit array plus a few hash functions that tells you an item is definitely not in a set or probably is — trading a controllable false-positive rate for enormous memory savings.
